criteria: `bytesize.py` implements two functions: `format_size(count)`, which returns a `str`, and `parse_size(text)`, which returns an `int`.
`format_size(count)` takes `count` as an `int` number of bytes and uses the units `B`, `KiB`, `MiB`, `GiB` and `TiB`, each 1024 times the one before.
`format_size` returns the count and `B` with no decimal for counts below 1024 bytes, for example `"0 B"` and `"1023 B"`.
`format_size` returns, from 1024 bytes on, a value with exactly one decimal and the largest unit in which the value is at least 1, for example `"1.0 KiB"` and `"1.5 KiB"`.
`format_size` rounds the value to one decimal, and an exact half rounds away from zero: 1280 bytes (exactly 1.25 KiB) gives `"1.3 KiB"`, and 2304 bytes (2.25 KiB) gives `"2.3 KiB"`.

`format_size` uses the next unit when rounding gives `1024.0`: 1048575 bytes gives `"1.0 MiB"`, not `"1024.0 KiB"`. `TiB` is the last unit, so values of 1024 TiB and more stay in `TiB`, for example `"2048.0 TiB"`.
`format_size` formats a negative count as its absolute value with a leading `-`, for example `"-1.5 KiB"`.
`format_size` raises `TypeError` when given a `bool` or a value that is not an `int`.

`parse_size(text)` accepts a number, optional spaces, and a unit, for example `"1.5 KiB"`, `"1.5KiB"` and `"10 B"`. Spaces around the whole text are ignored. Units are matched exactly as written (`B`, `KiB`, `MiB`, `GiB`, `TiB`), and `kib` and `KB` are invalid.
`parse_size` accepts a number made of digits with an optional fraction of one or more digits and an optional leading `-`. A fraction is not allowed with the unit `B`.
`parse_size` returns the exact number of bytes when that is a whole number and raises `ValueError` when it is not: `"0.5 KiB"` gives 512, and `"0.1 KiB"` raises `ValueError`.
`parse_size` raises `ValueError` for any other text.
The provided tests in test_visible.py pass, with that file unchanged
